s: A river leaving steep hills deposits its coarse load at the break of slope and spreads it in the form of a fan or cone. This landform is known as:
o: Floodplain
Alluvial fan
Natural levee
Delta
x: An alluvial fan forms where a river emerges from steep hills and loses velocity, depositing coarse material in a fan-shaped spread.
tq: Use the process of formation to identify the landform.
sec: Depositional landforms of rivers - fans, levees, floodplains, braided channels, deltas, oxbows, terraces  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Natural levee — Raised bank formed by deposition along the channel edge
Floodplain — Coarse gravel belt at the foot of the Himalayas
Braided channel — Single deep channel without riverine islands
Delta — Depositional feature formed at the break of slope
x: A natural levee is a raised bank built by sand deposited along the edges of a river channel. The other descriptions refer to bhabar, braided channels and alluvial fans respectively.
tq: Match each landform with its formation process and location.
sec: Depositional landforms of rivers - fans, levees, floodplains, braided channels, deltas, oxbows, terraces  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following statements about riverine landforms:
1. A floodplain is built by fine alluvium deposited when a river overflows.
2. A delta is formed at the mouth where a river meets the sea.
3. A braided channel is formed when sand deposits divide the channel into several parallel threads.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: All three statements are correct. Floodplains, deltas and braided channels are formed through distinct depositional processes described in the statements.
tq: Test several closely related depositional processes through coded combinations.
sec: Depositional landforms of rivers - fans, levees, floodplains, braided channels, deltas, oxbows, terraces  [APPSC]

s: With reference to an oxbow lake, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: It is formed when a river deposits material only at its mouth.
It is a lake formed in a glacial cirque.
It is the stagnant water left after a meander loop is cut off.
It is a deep channel formed by vertical erosion in the upper course.
x: Deposition on the concave side of a meander can steepen and narrow the loop until it is cut off, leaving stagnant water known as an oxbow lake.
tq: Follow the sequence of formation rather than identifying the feature by appearance alone.
sec: Depositional landforms of rivers - fans, levees, floodplains, braided channels, deltas, oxbows, terraces  [APPSC]

s: In a meandering river, which of the following correctly describes the two sides of a bend?
o: The outer bend is erosional and concave, while the inner slip-off side is depositional and convex.
The outer bend is depositional and convex, while the inner bend is erosional and concave.
The outer bend is depositional and straight, while the inner bend is erosional and steep.
Both bends are erosional and concave.
x: The outer, concave bend experiences erosion and forms a cliff, whereas the inner, convex slip-off side receives deposition.
tq: Use the reversed outer-bend and inner-bend comparison as the key distinction.
sec: Depositional landforms of rivers - fans, levees, floodplains, braided channels, deltas, oxbows, terraces  [APPSC]

s: Which of the following statements regarding river terraces is NOT correct?
o: Unpaired terraces necessarily occur at the same height on both banks.
They are formed when a stream cuts vertically into its own floodplain.
Paired terraces occur at the same height on both banks.
They represent former valley-floor or floodplain levels.
x: Unpaired terraces occur on one bank only, often in areas of slow uplift. Paired terraces, not unpaired terraces, occur at the same height on both banks.
tq: Find the statement that reverses the paired and unpaired terrace distinction.
sec: Depositional landforms of rivers - fans, levees, floodplains, braided channels, deltas, oxbows, terraces  [APPSC]

s: Why are river terraces listed among erosional landforms in the NCERT classification?
o: They are formed exclusively by wind erosion.
They are created by deposition at the river mouth.
They are made of marine sediments deposited along the coast.
They are produced by the down-cutting of a stream into its former floodplain.
x: Although terraces mark former floodplain levels, their formation involves vertical down-cutting by the stream, so they are treated as erosional landforms.
tq: Distinguish the origin of a feature from the material or surface it preserves.
sec: Depositional landforms of rivers - fans, levees, floodplains, braided channels, deltas, oxbows, terraces  [APPSC]

s: In the context of depositional activity by Himalayan rivers, which combination is appropriate?
o: Waterfalls, rapids and gorges
Braided channels, alluvial fans and natural levees
Canyons, deltas and potholes
Terraces, canyons and potholes
x: Braided channels, alluvial fans and natural levees are depositional features. Terraces are excluded in this classification because they result from vertical down-cutting.
tq: Separate depositional features from erosional features before selecting the combination.
sec: Depositional landforms of rivers - fans, levees, floodplains, braided channels, deltas, oxbows, terraces  [APPSC]

s: The belt of coarse gravel and pebbles deposited by Himalayan rivers where they enter the plains is called:
o: Bhabar
Bhangar
Khadar
Terai
x: Bhabar is the coarse gravel and pebble belt at the foothills where Himalayan rivers enter the plains.
tq: Discriminate among the closely related Himalayan foothill and plain terms.
sec: River-plain terms (doab, bhabar, khadar, prayag) and plain types  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following correctly describes the Terai?
o: An older alluvial surface containing kankar
The active floodplain containing only coarse gravel
A marshy and forested belt south of the Bhabar where streams reappear
A confluence of two or more rivers
x: The Terai lies south of the Bhabar and is a marshy, forested belt where streams that disappeared into the Bhabar come back to the surface.
tq: Use the north-to-south relation and stream behaviour to separate Terai from Bhabar.
sec: River-plain terms (doab, bhabar, khadar, prayag) and plain types  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Bhangar consists of older alluvium above the flood level.
2. Kankar or lime nodules are associated with Bhangar.
3. Khadar is the new alluvium of the active floodplain.
4. Khadar generally contains kankar but no fine clay or sand.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false because khadar consists of fine clay and sand and lacks kankar.
tq: Identify the single reversed characteristic in the Bhangar–Khadar comparison.
sec: River-plain terms (doab, bhabar, khadar, prayag) and plain types  [APPSC]

s: Devprayag is significant in physical geography because it is the place where:
o: The Bhagirathi and Alaknanda meet and the Ganga begins
The Yamuna enters the Indo-Ganga plain
The Chambal ravines are formed
The Brahmaputra enters India through a gorge
x: Devprayag is the confluence of the Bhagirathi and Alaknanda; from this confluence the river is known as the Ganga.
tq: Link the named confluence with the rivers meeting there and the resulting river.
sec: River-plain terms (doab, bhabar, khadar, prayag) and plain types  [APPSC]

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Alluvial plain — Indo-Ganga-Brahmaputra plain
Lacustrine plain — Active floodplain with annual deposition
Floodplain — Filled lake bed
Peneplain — Newly deposited fan at the mountain foot
x: The Indo-Ganga-Brahmaputra plain is an alluvial plain and is India's youngest physiographic division. A lacustrine plain is formed from filled lake beds, while a floodplain corresponds to khadar.
tq: Match plain types with their modes of origin and representative examples.
sec: River-plain terms (doab, bhabar, khadar, prayag) and plain types  [APPSC]

s: The Peninsular Plateau is described as a:
o: Lacustrine plain formed entirely from lake deposits
Young alluvial floodplain
Rejuvenated peneplain
Bhabar belt formed by Himalayan gravel
x: A peneplain is a nearly featureless surface produced by prolonged erosion, and the Peninsular Plateau is described as a rejuvenated peneplain.
tq: Identify the geomorphological term from the stated stage of erosion and rejuvenation.
sec: River-plain terms (doab, bhabar, khadar, prayag) and plain types  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following is the correct sequence of dominant river work from the upper course to the lower course?
o: Deposition — lateral erosion — vertical erosion
Lateral erosion — deposition — vertical erosion
Vertical erosion — lateral erosion and transport — deposition
Transport — vertical erosion — deposition and uplift
x: The upper course is dominated by vertical erosion, the middle course by lateral erosion and transport, and the lower course by deposition.
tq: Arrange river processes according to the downstream course sequence.
sec: River profile - upper, middle, lower course features  [APPSC]

s: Which of the following combinations is characteristic of the upper or youthful course of a river?
o: V-shaped valleys, waterfalls, rapids and potholes
Broad floodplains, levees and oxbow lakes
Deltas, estuaries and braided channels only
Wide meanders and extensive natural levees
x: The youthful upper course has a steep gradient and strong vertical erosion, producing V-shaped valleys, gorges, canyons, waterfalls, rapids and potholes.
tq: Recognise the youthful-course feature cluster rather than an isolated feature.
sec: River profile - upper, middle, lower course features  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following statements about the middle course of a river:
1. Lateral erosion and transport are important processes.
2. Valleys become wider than in the upper course.
3. Meanders may develop.
4. Vertical erosion is the sole dominant work.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
x: The middle course is marked by lateral erosion, transport, widening valleys and the development of meanders. Vertical erosion is not its sole dominant process.
tq: Reject the absolute word ‘sole’ while retaining the characteristic middle-course features.
sec: River profile - upper, middle, lower course features  [APPSC]

s: A river flowing through a gentle-gradient region develops broad floodplains, natural levees and oxbow lakes. These features indicate its:
o: Middle course only
Upper course
Lower course
Source region before the youthful stage
x: The lower or old-age course has a gentle gradient and is dominated by deposition, producing broad floodplains, levees and oxbow lakes.
tq: Infer the river stage from the dominant landform assemblage.
sec: River profile - upper, middle, lower course features  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following is NOT normally associated with the lower course of a river?
o: Broad floodplain
Delta or estuary
Pothole
Natural levee
x: Potholes are typical of the erosional upper course. Broad floodplains, levees and deltas or estuaries are associated with the lower course.
tq: Find the upper-course erosional feature among lower-course depositional features.
sec: River profile - upper, middle, lower course features  [APPSC]

s: A canyon is formed predominantly in which course of a river?
o: Lower course
Mouth or deltaic course
Upper course
Middle course
x: A canyon is an upper-course feature produced by strong vertical erosion in a river's youthful stage.
tq: Associate the landform with the river stage in which vertical erosion dominates.
sec: River profile - upper, middle, lower course features  [APPSC]

s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a gorge from a canyon?
o: A gorge is always wider at the top, whereas a canyon has equal width throughout.
A gorge has step-like sedimentary sides, whereas a canyon has straight sides in hard rock.
A gorge is almost equally wide at top and bottom, whereas a canyon is wider at the top.
A gorge is formed only by deposition, whereas a canyon is formed by marine erosion.
x: A gorge is a deep valley with very steep or straight sides and nearly equal width at top and bottom. A canyon has step-like sides and is wider at the top than at the bottom.
tq: Compare the width and side-slope characteristics rather than relying on the names alone.
sec: Gorge vs canyon (Grand Canyon)  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following statements regarding gorges and canyons:
1. Gorges generally form in hard rocks.
2. Canyons generally form in horizontally bedded sedimentary rocks.
3. A canyon is regarded as a variant of a gorge.
4. A gorge is an extended form of a canyon.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 reverses the relationship: a canyon is a variant of a gorge, not the reverse.
tq: Watch for the reversed relationship in a confusable pair.
sec: Gorge vs canyon (Grand Canyon)  [APPSC]

s: The Brahmaputra enters India through the Dihang gorge, which is associated with the:
o: Gandikota gorge on the Penna
Yarlung Tsangpo Grand Canyon near Namcha Barwa
Chambal badland region
Colorado River canyon in the United States
x: The Dihang gorge is associated with the Yarlung Tsangpo Grand Canyon near Namcha Barwa, where the Brahmaputra enters India.
tq: Separate similarly named Indian and international canyon or gorge features by river and location.
sec: Gorge vs canyon (Grand Canyon)  [APPSC]

s: Gandikota gorge, popularly called the ‘Grand Canyon of India’, is located on the:
o: Krishna River in Guntur district
Chambal River in Madhya Pradesh
Godavari River in East Godavari district
Penna River in YSR Kadapa district
x: Gandikota gorge is situated on the Penna River in YSR Kadapa district and is popularly known as the Grand Canyon of India.
tq: Use the river–region association to distinguish Indian gorge locations.
sec: Gorge vs canyon (Grand Canyon)  [APPSC]

s:
Arrange the following stages in the development of a gully network in the correct order:
A. Formation of badland topography
B. Gathering of overland flow into rills
C. Deepening and enlargement into gullies
D. Merging of rills
o: B, D, C, A
D, B, C, A
B, C, D, A
A, B, D, C
x: Overland flow first gathers into rills; the rills merge, deepen into gullies, and a dense network of gullies produces badland topography.
tq: Follow the first-to-last geomorphic process sequence.
sec: Ravines and badland topography → region  [APPSC]

s: A gully is best described as a:
o: Former floodplain left above the present valley floor
Water-worn channel formed in a semi-arid area
Raised bank formed by river deposition
Fan-shaped deposit at the foot of a mountain
x: A gully is a water-worn channel of semi-arid areas formed when overland flow gathers into rills that merge and deepen.
tq: Identify the exact geomorphological definition rather than the larger landscape produced by it.
sec: Ravines and badland topography → region  [APPSC]

s: Which region is classically associated with India's badland topography?
o: Western coastal plain
Chambal basin
Godavari delta
Rann of Kutch
x: The ravines of the Chambal valley in Central India form India's classic badland topography. The Chos of Hoshiarpur in Punjab are another example.
tq: Use the region-specific association to distinguish badlands from coastal, deltaic and saline landscapes.
sec: Ravines and badland topography → region  [APPSC]

s: The ‘Chos’ associated with ravine and badland topography are found in:
o: Hoshiarpur, Punjab
YSR Kadapa, Andhra Pradesh
Namcha Barwa, Tibet
The Kashmir Valley
x: The Chos of Hoshiarpur in Punjab are identified as another region of ravine and badland topography besides the Chambal valley.
tq: Test the less prominent regional example rather than the most famous one.
sec: Ravines and badland topography → region  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with an arcuate delta?
o: Nile — arcuate delta
Mississippi — arcuate delta
Tiber — arcuate delta
Narmada — arcuate delta
x: The Nile forms an arcuate or fan-shaped delta. The Mississippi forms a bird's-foot delta, the Tiber a cuspate delta, and the Narmada an estuarine mouth.
tq: Use the river-example association to distinguish closely related delta types.
sec: Delta types → river examples, largest delta, conditions for formation

s: A delta characterised by long, branching distributaries extending into the sea is known as a:
o: Cuspate delta
Estuarine delta
Bird's-foot delta
Arcuate delta
x: A bird's-foot delta has long, branching distributaries projecting into the sea; the Mississippi is the standard example given.
tq: Identify the landform from its distinctive shape and distributary pattern.
sec: Delta types → river examples, largest delta, conditions for formation

s: The cuspate delta is best represented by which one of the following river examples?
o: Mississippi
Krishna
Tiber
Nile
x: The Tiber in Italy forms a cuspate delta, which is tooth- or cusp-shaped.
tq: Test the exact river-example pair rather than relying only on shape.
sec: Delta types → river examples, largest delta, conditions for formation

s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Cuspate — Tiber
Arcuate — Nile
Bird's-foot — Mississippi
Estuarine — Godavari
x: Godavari forms a delta, whereas Narmada and Tapi are the examples of estuarine mouths listed here.
tq: Find the mismatched river and delta type.
sec: Delta types → river examples, largest delta, conditions for formation

s:
Consider the following statements regarding delta formation:
1. A river must carry a heavy load of sediment.
2. The sea near the river mouth should preferably be shallow.
3. Strong tides and currents favour the accumulation of a delta.
4. The river flow should be sufficiently slow and steady for silt to settle.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1, 2 and 4 only
1 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
x: Heavy sediment load, shallow coastal water, and sufficiently slow and steady flow favour delta formation. Strong tides and currents generally remove sediment and do not favour delta accumulation.
tq: Separate the positive depositional conditions from the reversed tide-and-current statement.
sec: Delta types → river examples, largest delta, conditions for formation

s: Why do not all rivers form deltas at their mouths?
o: Because river mouths are always occupied by waterfalls
Because all rivers lose their water before reaching the sea
Because delta formation requires suitable sediment, coastal and current conditions
Because deltas form only in glaciated valleys
x: Delta formation depends on adequate sediment load, shallow sea, weak tides and currents, and sufficiently slow deposition-friendly flow; therefore every river does not form a delta.
tq: Apply the necessary-condition approach to an exception-based geographical process.
sec: Delta types → river examples, largest delta, conditions for formation

s: The west-flowing rivers of the Deccan generally form estuaries rather than deltas mainly because they:
o: carry no water during the monsoon season
are affected by exceptionally strong tides throughout their courses
have steep gradients, hard-rock courses and short courses
flow through extensive alluvial plains with very low gradients
x: The west-flowing Deccan rivers commonly have steep gradients, hard-rock channels and short courses, conditions that favour estuaries rather than extensive deltas.
tq: Link the landform outcome with the controlling relief and river-course conditions.
sec: Delta types → river examples, largest delta, conditions for formation

s: An estuary is best described as:
o: A distributary network separated completely from the sea
A partly enclosed river mouth with a free connection to the sea
A river valley cut only by glacial erosion
A closed lake formed behind a sand bar
x: An estuary is a partly enclosed river mouth that retains a free connection with the sea and functions as an ecotone.
tq: Discriminate between the precise definitions of delta, lagoon and estuary.
sec: Delta types → river examples, largest delta, conditions for formation

s: Most estuaries were formed in association with:
o: Permian glaciation
Holocene sea-level rise
Complete tectonic closure of the sea
Desertification of river basins
x: Most estuaries developed during the Holocene as rising sea levels drowned lower river valleys while retaining a connection with the sea.
tq: Associate the coastal feature with its geological time and formative process.
sec: Delta types → river examples, largest delta, conditions for formation

s: The Sundarbans are associated with which of the following?
o: The Narmada estuary and the world's largest freshwater lake
The Tiber delta and the world's largest coniferous forest
The Ganga-Brahmaputra delta and the world's largest mangrove forest
The Mississippi delta and the world's largest coral reef
x: The Ganga-Brahmaputra delta includes the Sundarbans, recognised as the world's largest mangrove forest.
tq: Connect the delta, regional name and ecological feature in one precise association.
sec: Delta types → river examples, largest delta, conditions for formation

s: A V-shaped valley develops through the sequence of:
o: Cirques, arêtes and horns produced by glacial plucking
Rills, gullies and valleys produced mainly by vertical erosion
Meanders, oxbow lakes and deltas produced only by lateral erosion
Dunes, beaches and spits produced mainly by marine deposition
x: Rills enlarge into gullies and then valleys through predominantly vertical erosion, producing a V-shaped valley.
tq: Recognise the erosional sequence leading to a named valley form.
sec: Erosional landforms (V-shaped valley, waterfall, potholes, incised meanders)

s: Potholes in a river bed are primarily formed when:
o: Fine silt settles in stagnant water and builds circular mounds
Rock fragments whirled by eddies grind and drill circular holes
Sea waves deposit pebbles at the river mouth
Groundwater dissolves limestone beneath a river
x: Eddies rotate rock fragments in depressions, causing abrasion that drills circular potholes into the bedrock.
tq: Identify the process rather than merely memorising the landform name.
sec: Erosional landforms (V-shaped valley, waterfall, potholes, incised meanders)

s: A large pothole-like depression situated below a waterfall is called a:
o: Structural basin
Natural levee
Plunge pool
Cuspate delta
x: A plunge pool is the large erosional depression formed below a waterfall by the impact and turbulence of falling water.
tq: Distinguish a specialised form of pothole from other fluvial and structural features.
sec: Erosional landforms (V-shaped valley, waterfall, potholes, incised meanders)

s: Waterfalls commonly develop where a river crosses:
o: A flat interfluve far from any channel
Only a broad zone of unconsolidated sand
A resistant rock band or a fault step
A perfectly uniform layer of soft alluvium
x: A waterfall may form where differential resistance creates a resistant rock band or where a fault produces a step in the river profile.
tq: Match the erosional feature with its structural or lithological setting.
sec: Erosional landforms (V-shaped valley, waterfall, potholes, incised meanders)

s: Incised or entrenched meanders are most likely to form when:
o: A river is diverted into a newly formed coastal lagoon
Uplift rejuvenates a river and its meanders cut deeply into hard rock
A river loses all its gradient and deposits silt in a shallow sea
Strong tides reverse the direction of river flow
x: When uplift rejuvenates a river, renewed vertical erosion may incise pre-existing meanders deeply into resistant bedrock.
tq: Infer the landform from the interaction of rejuvenation, uplift and vertical erosion.
sec: Erosional landforms (V-shaped valley, waterfall, potholes, incised meanders)

s: Which one of the following drainage patterns develops over relatively uniform rock and has a tree-like appearance?
o: Radial
Trellis
Dendritic
Annular
x: Dendritic drainage develops over relatively uniform rock and resembles the branching form of a tree; it is characteristic of the northern plains.
tq: Use the controlling rock condition and visual pattern together.
sec: Drainage patterns → examples

s: The trellis drainage pattern is generally associated with:
o: A central depression into which all streams flow
Folded rocks, where tributaries join the main streams at right angles
An eroded dome with concentric rings of hard and soft rocks
A central high from which all streams flow outward
x: Trellis drainage develops in folded terrain, with tributaries commonly joining the main streams at right angles; the Appalachians provide an example.
tq: Distinguish drainage patterns by their structural control and tributary angle.
sec: Drainage patterns → examples

s: A drainage system in which streams flow outward from a central high is termed:
o: Dendritic
Radial
Centripetal
Rectangular
x: Radial drainage develops around a central elevated area. Amarkantak is an Indian example, with the Narmada, Son and Mahanadi flowing from the region.
tq: Use the direction of stream flow from or towards the centre to split the options.
sec: Drainage patterns → examples

s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Centripetal drainage — Loktak Lake, Manipur
Radial drainage — Mississippi Delta
Trellis drainage — Sundarbans
Annular drainage — northern alluvial plains
x: Centripetal drainage carries streams towards a central depression, as in the Loktak Lake basin of Manipur.
tq: Start from the sure example-location pair and eliminate mismatched drainage settings.
sec: Drainage patterns → examples

s: Rectangular drainage is typically controlled by:
o: Joints and faults, producing right-angle bends
A single central volcanic cone only
Uniform unconsolidated alluvium without structural control
A drowned funnel-shaped river mouth
x: Rectangular drainage develops where joints and faults guide stream courses, producing frequent right-angle bends, especially on joint-controlled plateaus.
tq: Match the geometric pattern with the geological control responsible for it.
sec: Drainage patterns → examples

s: Annular drainage is associated with:
o: A central depression surrounded by inward-flowing streams
Folded mountains with parallel ridges only
Eroded domes containing rings of hard and soft rock
A uniform plain with no lithological variation
x: Annular drainage follows alternating concentric bands of hard and soft rock around an eroded structural dome.
tq: Identify the structural landform underlying a concentric drainage pattern.
sec: Drainage patterns → examples

s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Dendritic — rivers of the northern plains
2. Trellis — Appalachians
3. Radial — Amarkantak
4. Centripetal — Loktak Lake
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
o: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
x: All four pairs are correctly matched: dendritic drainage occurs in the northern plains, trellis drainage in the Appalachians, radial drainage at Amarkantak, and centripetal drainage at Loktak Lake.
tq: Check each example against the defining direction or structural setting before choosing the complete combination.
sec: Drainage patterns → examples

s: Stream capture, also called river piracy, occurs when:
o: A tributary changes from a dendritic to an annular pattern
A lake drains through a newly formed coastal delta
A river deposits sediment until its mouth is completely blocked
A stream erodes headward, breaches a neighbouring basin and diverts its upper waters
x: In stream capture, headward erosion allows one stream to breach the divide of a neighbouring basin and divert the upper course of the captured stream.
tq: Test the process sequence: headward erosion, basin breach and diversion.
sec: Stream capture, graded profile, base level terms

s: A graded river profile is one in which:
o: The river flows upward from its mouth to its source
The river consists entirely of waterfalls and rapids
The long profile is smoothly concave and erosion and deposition are broadly balanced
Deposition has completely stopped along the whole channel
x: A graded profile is a smooth, generally concave long profile in which erosion and deposition are sufficiently balanced over time.
tq: Distinguish the equilibrium profile from absolute absence of erosion or deposition.
sec: Stream capture, graded profile, base level terms

s: Which one of the following represents the ultimate base level of a river?
o: The nearest drainage divide
Sea level
The upper limit of the floodplain
The highest point of the river basin
x: Base level is the lowest level to which a river can erode, and sea level is regarded as the ultimate base level.
tq: Apply the definition of the lowest attainable erosional level.
sec: Stream capture, graded profile, base level terms

s:
Which of the following can act as a local base level for a river?
1. A lake
2. A dam
3. The sea
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: Lakes and dams can provide local base levels, while sea level is the ultimate base level; therefore all three can be base-level controls in the stated sense.
tq: Separate local base levels from the ultimate base level without treating them as mutually exclusive.
sec: Stream capture, graded profile, base level terms

s: A drainage divide is best defined as:
o: The deepest part of a river channel
The point where a river enters the sea
A depositional bar dividing a delta into distributaries
A ridge separating two drainage basins
x: A drainage divide is an elevated ridge or interfluve that separates neighbouring drainage basins.
tq: Discriminate between a basin boundary and channel or mouth features.
sec: Stream capture, graded profile, base level terms

s: Which statement correctly compares drainage divides in young and old relief?
o: They are equally sharp in all types of relief
They are absent in both the Himalaya and old plateaus
They are generally sharp in the Himalaya and faint on old plateaus
They are faint in the Himalaya and sharp on old plateaus
x: Young, rugged Himalayan relief produces sharp drainage divides, whereas prolonged erosion on old plateaus tends to make divides less distinct or faint.
tq: Use the age-and-relief comparison to identify the reversed statement.
sec: Stream capture, graded profile, base level terms

s:
Consider the following statements about sinking deltas:
1. Seven major deltas together account for about 57% of the world's sinking delta area.
2. Deltas cover about 1% of the world's land area.
3. Deltas support approximately 6% of the world's population.
